title: Bram and the Summer
premise: Silas Ravensworth has spent nine years keeping his world small: a daughter, a bookshop, and a grief he refuses to name. When the deed to the town's dying orchard surfaces bearing both his late husband's name and that of Bram Calloway—the man who left them both—Silas learns the orchard was left jointly to the two people its owner loved most, and it will be sold unless they can hold it together through one summer. Forced into proximity by legal necessity and his daughter Wren's quiet hunger for family, Silas watches power corrupt the town councilmen circling the land and discovers how far he'll go to protect what's his. The climax comes when Silas must choose between exposing a betrayal that would save the orchard and destroying Bram in the process; he chooses honesty instead, losing the orchard but winning something harder. The book ends with the last train of summer leaving without either of them on it, the two men planting new trees on ground they no longer own but refuse to abandon.
about_author: Edmund Joubert is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who spent fifteen years shelving other people's love stories before writing his own. He lives near an abandoned orchard and writes at dawn, when the light forgives everything.

chapters.title: The Deed in the Drawer
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. While cataloguing a dead woman's donated books, Silas finds a deed naming him and one estranged name he hasn't spoken aloud in nine years as joint heirs to Hollow Orchard. The emotional beat is dread disguised as irritation—he burns to throw it away, but Wren sees the name over his shoulder.

chapters.title: A Stranger Buys a Paperback
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram returns to town broke and uninvited, intending only to sign papers and leave, and walks into Silas's shop pretending to be a customer. Their brittle politeness cracks when Wren recognizes him instantly. The beat is the terrible tenderness of being known by someone you wronged.

chapters.title: Terms of Coexistence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A lawyer explains the deed's condition: joint stewardship for one full season or the land reverts to the county. Councilman Aldous Vetch offers Bram cash to walk away. The beat is reluctant alliance—two men agreeing to share a fence line and nothing else.

chapters.title: Wren's Map
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Twelve-year-old Wren, who has never had a father figure who stayed, begins secretly mapping the orchard with Bram, cataloguing trees her Papa once loved. Silas discovers the map and feels betrayed twice over. The beat is jealousy wearing the mask of protection.

chapters.title: What Vetch Wants
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas uncovers Vetch's plan: a resort development requiring the orchard parcel, and evidence Vetch forged the county's original survey years ago. Power shows its first teeth. The beat is the seduction of leverage—Silas realizes he could destroy Vetch, if he's willing to burn things down.

chapters.title: Cider and Confession
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Pressing the first apples alone, Bram finally tells Silas why he left: not infidelity, but cowardice after the accident that killed their friend. Grief they've both carried separately becomes shared. The beat is the fragile warmth of a truth told too late.

chapters.title: The Offer on the Table
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Vetch raises his offer and adds a threat: expose Silas's unpaid back taxes or lose the shop itself. Bram urges fighting dirty; Silas refuses to become what he hates. First real fight between them. The beat is the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Fire Season
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A suspicious fire guts half the orchard the night before the council vote; all evidence points to Vetch's hired man, but proof is thin. Wren is nearly hurt saving the deed box. The beat is terror crystallizing into resolve—Silas stops being invisible.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. At the climactic hearing, Silas holds the forged-survey evidence that would convict Vetch—but using it means revealing Bram signed a false affidavit under pressure, destroying him publicly. Silas chooses truth over victory: he testifies about everything, including his own silence for nine years. The orchard is lost; Vetch falls anyway. The beat is costly integrity.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, closing with Wren. Autumn arrives; the orchard belongs to the county now, but nobody stops the three of them from planting saplings on the dead rows. Bram misses the last train out on purpose. The beat is quiet resolution: family isn't found, it's kept—and some ground you keep even when you don't own it.
